paras: The beating of Daniel Allen at the Seamen's Union was an assault on a West Indian Black seaman by a union agent and several white members at a West street branch in New York City on Tuesday, September 15, 1903. Black members drove the white men from the rooms, and no arrests were made. The New York Sun presented the fight as the outbreak of a growing split between white and Black union members over jobs.
According to the Sun, Black members complained that whites were always chosen when members volunteered to ship on a vessel.

Allen, who had been wrecked on the schooner Nellie T. Moore, went to the West street branch to claim his shipwreck fee and showed his union credentials. Unable to make the agent understand his claim, he cursed him, and the agent "promptly made for him." According to the Black members, the agent tried to throw Allen downstairs while several white members joined in and "rained blows on the negro's head."
Black members came up from the saloon below on hearing his cries and, outnumbering the whites two to one, drove them into the street before the police arrived.

No arrests were made, and the coverage does not say whether Allen was hurt. The Sun reported "broad hints" that Black seamen might form their own union; no one at the Atlantic Coast Seamen's Union office would comment.

The only account of the fight ran in the New York Sun on September 20 under "TROUBLE IN SEAMEN'S UNION / NEGROES ARE THINKING OF BREAKING AWAY FROM IT." The Sun gave the Black members' complaints at length and quoted ship owner Fields S. Pendleton, who said the union's foreign-born agents favored their own countrymen over Black members. The same article described Allen's "West Indian curses" and the Black members' celebration upstairs as a "ward dance."
On September 25 the Portland Daily Press in Maine reprinted the discrimination complaints and Pendleton's statement from the New York Journal of Commerce, omitting the fight.

reader.title: Beating of Daniel Allen at the Seamen's Union
bases: A1 describes a fight inside a Seamen's Union branch office, in which the agent and several white members beat a Black member who was claiming a shipwreck fee, set within a racial split over job assignment in the union; no crowd from outside took part.
Only the New York Sun (A1) reports the fight, and it attributes the beating to 'the negroes'; the Portland reprint (A2, A3) carries only the background on union discrimination.

accounts.label: Black union members (as reported by the Sun)
accounts.gist: The agent tried to throw Allen downstairs and several white members beat him about the head until Black members came up from the saloon and drove the whites out.

accounts.label: Union agent and white members
accounts.gist: No version from the agent or the white members appears; the union office declined to comment.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'TROUBLE IN SEAMEN'S UNION / NEGROES ARE THINKING OF BREAKING AWAY FROM IT,' gave the Black members' complaints of discrimination at length, but described Allen's 'West Indian curses' and the Black members' 'ward [war] dance.'
The Portland Daily Press reprinted the discrimination story from the New York Journal of Commerce under 'SEAMEN'S UNION TROUBLE' without the account of the fight.

record_check.dossier: A fight inside a union office between the agent and white members and a Black member, framed as a labor and racial split within the union; 'labor' fits better than a mob assault.
The branch agent (unnamed) and several white union members.
Fellow union members and the union agent, not a crowd.
Consistent: 'Tuesday afternoon' in the Sunday, September 20 Sun.

sources.note: Only account of the fight: Allen, 'a West Indian black', beaten by the agent and white members at a West street union branch; Black members drove the whites out; no arrests; set within complaints of union discrimination.
quotes: Daniel Allen, a West Indian black, went to claim his shipwreck fee, having been wrecked on the schooner Nellie T. Moore.
According to the negroes, the agent tried to throw Allen downstairs, while several white members of the union joined the agent and rained blows on the negro's head.
They quieted down before the police got there. No arrests were made.
At present the union discriminates against the blacks by refusing to give them employment, notwithstanding the fact that they are members of the union.
